title: How Does Youth Ministry Form Faith That Survives College?
subtitle: On forming teenagers in a faith that survives college, moving beyond entertainment to discipleship, parents, and the slow work of formation

sections.title: The Question No Youth Pamphlet Asks
sections.body:
We measure youth ministry by the wrong things. We count the bodies on the trip, the noise in the room, the photos of the lock-in. Then the same kids graduate, leave for college, and a heartbreaking share of them never come back.

We were so busy keeping them entertained that we forgot to make them disciples.

A generation of youth ministry built itself on the assumption that if church was fun enough, teenagers would stay. They did not stay. You cannot compete with the world at being fun, and a faith that was only ever fun has nothing to offer a twenty year old in a dorm room at two in the morning asking whether any of it is true. I am not against laughter or pizza or the loud game. I am against handing a child a faith too small to hold his adult grief. We owe these kids more than a good Friday night. We owe them something that will still be standing when their life falls in.

sections.title: Stop Talking Down to Them
sections.body:
Teenagers can tell when they are being condescended to, and nothing closes a young heart faster. They are wrestling with death, sex, meaning, justice, and their own breaking families, and we hand them a cartoon and a moral.

Give them the deep end. They are drowning in the shallow one.

The research on this is plain enough that even those of us who resist it should listen. Young people keep the faith that took them seriously, that gave them a robust theology, that let them ask the hardest questions out loud without panic. So teach them doctrine, real doctrine, the kind their parents were never given. Let them argue. Let them doubt in the room instead of alone on a screen. Tell them the cost of following Christ before they sign up, the way Jesus always did. The teenager handed a serious faith may rebel against it for a season, but he has something to come back to. The teenager handed a mascot has nothing to return to at all.

sections.title: The Parents Are the Real Youth Ministry
sections.body:
Here is the truth that puts most youth budgets in their place. The single greatest predictor of a child's faith is not the youth program. It is whether the parents actually live what they claim on Sunday.

You get a few hours a week. The home gets the other hundred and sixty.

A youth ministry that ignores parents is bailing water while the hull stays cracked. The most strategic thing a youth pastor can do is not build a flashier event. It is to help mothers and fathers pray with their own children, read Scripture at their own tables, and confess their own failures honestly enough that faith looks survivable to a watching teenager. So train the parents. Send the lesson home so the dinner table can carry it. Tell the father he is the pastor of his own house whether he wanted the job or not. The youth ministry that disciples parents will outlast the one that only entertains their kids, every time.

sections.title: What They Remember Is Who Stayed
sections.body:
Ask grown believers what kept them in the faith through the hard years and they almost never name a program. They name a person. A leader who learned their name, came to their game, noticed when they were gone, and did not leave.

Kids do not need a crowd. They need a few adults who refuse to disappear.

The youth worker who lasts is not the most charismatic one on the stage. It is the one who is still texting the awkward kid in eleventh grade, still showing up after the funny ones moved on. Surround each teenager with a handful of grown believers who are not their parents and not paid to like them, who simply decide that this young life matters. That web of stubborn adult love is what carries a kid across the canyon of the college years. Build that, and you have built something a budget cut cannot destroy. Build only events, and you have built something that ends the day the music stops.

sections.title: You May Never See the Fruit
sections.body:
Youth ministry asks you to plant trees whose shade you will not sit under. The seeds you sow in a fifteen year old may not break ground until he is thirty, broken, and finally ready. By then you will be long gone, and someone else will get the joy of the harvest.

I have spent myself on kids who walked away, and lain awake certain I had failed. Years later, word reached me that some had come home.

That is the deal. We are not in the business of immediate results, and the youth pastor who needs to see the fruit to keep working is in the wrong field. We labor for a faith that outlives us in people who will outlive us. So pour yourself out and then let go, trusting the God who is the actual keeper of these children and who works on a clock we cannot read. Do not measure your ministry by who comes back this year. Measure it by whether you gave them a faith worth coming back to, and then leave the rest where it has always belonged, with the One who never loses what is sown in his name.
